natgas_bridge.current_policy: California still gets about 40% of its in-state electricity from natural gas, and gas heats most of its roughly 14 million homes. But the state is steering new buildings toward electric power instead. In 2022, the California Air Resources Board (CARB — the state's air-quality agency) set a goal: by 2030, every new furnace and water heater sold for homes should be zero-emission, with commercial buildings following by 2035. CARB is still writing the actual rule to make that happen. It scaled the rule back in December 2025, and a board vote is expected in 2026, but nothing is final yet. Meanwhile, dozens of cities banned gas in new construction after Berkeley did so in 2019 — until a 2023 federal appeals court ruling (CRA v. Berkeley) said federal appliance law overrides those local bans. So the state has shifted to using building codes and emissions standards instead.
key_facts: About 40% of California's electricity comes from natural gas, and gas heats most of the state's homes and water.
CARB's 2022 plan aims for 100% of new home furnaces and water heaters sold to be zero-emission by 2030 — but the rule to enforce it isn't finished, and was scaled back in December 2025.
A 2023 federal appeals court ruling (CRA v. Berkeley) said local bans on gas hookups in new buildings are overridden by federal appliance law.
California offers rebates for heat pumps (electric heating-and-cooling units) through TECH Clean California and utility programs, aiming for 6 million installed by 2030.

Aliso Canyon — the gas storage site of the 2015–16 SoCalGas methane blowout, the largest in U.S. history — is still running. A once-planned 2027 closure is now not expected until the late 2030s at the earliest.
natgas_bridge.comparison: California is one of the most aggressive states on switching buildings off gas, alongside New York (which banned gas in most new buildings starting 2026) and Washington. Most states have gone the other way: more than 20 have passed laws that bar cities from restricting natural gas hookups.
natgas_bridge.arguments_for_change: Supporters of moving off gas faster say buildings are a big source of greenhouse gases and smog-forming pollution, and that burning gas indoors raises health concerns. They argue that building new gas pipes and hookups is risky because that equipment could become worthless as the grid goes electric. They point out that heat pumps now beat gas furnaces in most California climates. And they warn that as fewer customers use gas, the fixed cost of maintaining the pipe network falls on the people left behind — often lower-income households — so a planned, orderly switch is cheaper than a chaotic one.
natgas_bridge.arguments_against_change: Supporters of keeping gas as a bridge say gas can be switched on instantly to back up solar and wind when those aren't available, helping prevent blackouts at peak demand. They argue that forcing everyone to go electric raises upfront costs for families and strains a grid that's already expensive. With California electricity rates the 2nd-highest in the nation, they say the money saved by running a heat pump is uncertain. And they warn that sudden mandates outrun the electrical-panel upgrades and trained workforce needed to install millions of heat pumps.

oil_gas.current_policy: California allows oil and gas drilling within the state, but it has tightened the rules and isn't approving much new drilling. [SB 1137](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB1137) (Gonzalez, 2022) bans new or reworked wells within 3,200 feet of homes, schools, hospitals, and other places where people spend a lot of time. The oil industry tried to overturn the law with a ballot referendum, but withdrew it on June 26, 2024 — so the buffer-zone law took effect instead of going to voters as a 2024 ballot measure. In-state oil production has dropped sharply: California pumped about 104 million barrels of crude in 2024, down roughly 70% from its peak. And CARB's Low Carbon Fuel Standard — a state rule that pushes transportation fuels to produce less carbon, amended in 2024 and effective July 2025 — keeps tightening those targets.
key_facts: [SB 1137](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB1137)'s 3,200-foot buffer between new wells and homes took effect June 27, 2024 after the industry withdrew its repeal referendum. It was NOT passed as a 'Prop 4' ballot measure — that's a common mix-up.
California produced about 104 million barrels of crude in 2024 — down roughly 70% from its peak. The state ranks about 7th among U.S. oil producers.
Kern County accounts for roughly 65–70% of California's in-state oil production.
California imports most of the crude its refineries use — only about a quarter comes from in-state wells. The rest arrives by sea or from Alaska.

CARB's 2024 update to the Low Carbon Fuel Standard (a rule that requires transportation fuels to get cleaner over time; effective July 1, 2025) tightened the targets. CARB estimated it would add about 5–8 cents per gallon in the near term, though some academic estimates were higher.
oil_gas.comparison: California is the only major U.S. oil-producing state that pairs large output with a stated plan to wind production down. Texas, New Mexico, and North Dakota are all expanding. California's 3,200-foot buffer between new wells and homes is among the largest required drilling setbacks in the country.
oil_gas.arguments_for_change: Supporters of phasing out oil faster say drilling concentrates air pollution and health harms in low-income and Latino communities near the wells. They note that in-state production is already shrinking and supplies only a minority of the crude California refines — so winding it down in an orderly way would have limited effect on supply. They argue that continued drilling clashes with the state's carbon-neutrality goal, and that every new well adds to the pile of abandoned, idle wells the state will eventually have to pay to clean up.
oil_gas.arguments_against_change: Supporters of keeping production say in-state oil supports tens of thousands of jobs and a big share of Kern County's tax base. They argue that cutting local supply means importing more crude — often produced under weaker environmental rules elsewhere — and leaves drivers exposed to price spikes. They warn that refinery closures already threaten fuel supply and prices, and that sudden restrictions push up gas prices in a state that already has among the nation's highest prices at the pump.

utility_rates.explainer: Most Californians get electricity from an 'investor-owned utility' (IOU) — a private company like PG&E, Southern California Edison, or SDG&E that answers to shareholders. Their prices are set by a state board, the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC), which decides what costs the companies can recover from customers. A few areas instead have public utilities, owned by the city or a public district. Electricity is billed per kilowatt-hour (kWh) — roughly the energy to run a microwave for an hour.
utility_rates.current_policy: California's three big investor-owned utilities — PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E — charge some of the highest electricity rates in the country. The federal Energy Information Administration puts the statewide average around 27 cents per kWh, second only to Hawaii. PG&E residential rates rose about 50% from 2020 to 2024, driven heavily by the cost of wildfire prevention and grid upgrades that the CPUC approved. In May 2024, carrying out [AB 205](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220AB205) (2022), the CPUC added an income-based fixed charge — a flat monthly fee tied to household income, about $24.15/month for most customers ($6 and $12 for low-income CARE/FERA enrollees). In exchange, the per-kWh rate is projected to drop 5–7 cents. It starts showing up on PG&E bills in early 2026.
key_facts: California's average electricity price is about 27 cents per kWh (per the federal EIA) — 2nd-highest among states, behind Hawaii.
PG&E residential rates rose about 50% from 2020 to 2024; households on the low-income CARE discount saw even steeper increases.
The CPUC's May 2024 income-based fixed charge is about $24.15/month (reduced to $6 or $12 for low-income tiers), in exchange for a 5–7 cents per kWh cut to usage-based rates; it rolls out in 2025–26.
Spending on wildfire prevention and grid hardening is a leading reason recent rate increases were approved.
Public utilities like SMUD (Sacramento) and LADWP (Los Angeles) usually charge well below IOU rates, fueling debate over public-power alternatives.
utility_rates.comparison: California's IOU rates are far above the U.S. average (around 17 cents per kWh) and most peer states; only Hawaii is consistently higher. Its income-based fixed charge is the first in the nation to tie part of the bill to a household's income instead of how much power it uses.
utility_rates.arguments_for_change: People who want stronger consumer protection argue that IOU rates have risen far faster than inflation while the utilities still earn guaranteed profits for shareholders. They say the CPUC too easily lets utilities pass wildfire and infrastructure costs to customers, and that high rates undercut the very switch to electric appliances and cars the state is requiring. They point to public utilities like SMUD, which deliver lower rates, as proof that structural reform — even having the public take over the utility — could cut bills.
utility_rates.arguments_against_change: People who defend the current cost-recovery approach argue that wildfire hardening, grid upgrades, and storm resilience are real, necessary costs that someone has to pay — and skimping on them risks blackouts and catastrophic fires. They say utilities need predictable profits to attract the money for those investments, and that aggressive rate caps could hurt reliability or just shift costs onto taxpayers. They add that targeted discounts (CARE/FERA) and the new income-based fixed charge already protect low-income customers without tearing up the whole system.
